A B S T R A C T
Marine accident investigation reports contain valuable vet underutilized information due to their unstructured
nature. While knowledge graphs (KGs) offer a promising solution for structured modeling and quantitative
reasoning based on these reports, the construction of high-quality, domain-specific KGs remains technically
challenging. To enable more efficient and scalable knowledge extraction in maritime safety domain, this study
proposes an automated pipeline based on large language models (LLMs) which enhances existing approaches by
customizing LLM prompting and evaluation frameworks. A chain-of-thought and one-shot prompting method is
adopted to identify critical hazardous factors and their coupling relationships. Besides, a comprehensive quality
assessment framework is developed to assess the accuracy and complexity of the generated KGs. Applied to real-
world accident reports from maritime authorities, the proposed LLM-based method demonstrates substantial
improvements in automation efficiency and extraction accuracy compared with traditional approaches.
Furthermore, the quality evaluation framework provides complementary indicators to traditional metrics by
reflecting the global semantic coherence and structural redundancy of the maritime safety KG. The findings offei
actionable insights for deploying LLM-based tools to support data-driven maritime risk analysis enhancing
transport safety management and decision making in complex operational environments.

2. Literature review
2.1. Marine accident analysis with knowledge graphs
Marine accidents are influenced by dynamic meteorological condi
tions (e.g., winds, waves and low visibility), vessel inherent defects, and
operational or management failures (Luo et al., 2024; Yang et al., 2024;
Ma et al., 2025). These incidents are often low in frequency but high in
consequence (Chen, P. et al., 2022). Compared to other operational data,
the accident records are sparse and predominantly unstructured, posing
challenges for traditional accident analytical models such as Fault Tree
Analysis (FTA) and Bayesian Network (BN) that demonstrate limitations
in semantical representation and nuanced information storage (Li et al.
2024; Xiong et al., 2024). To address these issues, KGs have emerged as a
promising approach for marine accident analysis.
KGs represent complex systems through networks of heterogeneous
entities, attributes, and relations, making them particularly well-suited
for modeling multi-factorial causes and cascading effects (Zarei et al.,
2022). To accurately represent the marine accident process, customized
concepts and entity types must be defined in addition to the general
entity types (e.g., person, location, time, and organizations) used in
open-domain tasks (Barron et al., 2024). For instance, Gan et al. (2023)
developed an ontology of ship collision accidents integrating
context-based and content-based metadata. Contextual elements, such
as accident descriptions, responsibility, and administrative advice, were
incorporated to preserve the original information of reports, while
content elements including involved ships, location, causes and conse
quences, were identified to reflect multi-dimensional perspective of the
accidents. Attributes of entities, such as the numerical hazard severity
level and the enumerated event types, were used to provide structured
variability across standardized entities (Zhu et al., 2024). As for re
lations, causal and spatial-temporal relationships are crucial in accident
causation modeling. Xie et al. (2024) employed causal and sequential
relations to link the vessel events and actions. Huang et al. (2025)
constructed causal chains to capture the causal and temporal dynamics
of event evolution in railway accidents.
By encoding the above elements into graphs, KGs transform
unstructured narratives into machine-readable, semantically rich for
mats while preserving much of the original contextual details. Despite
the promise, challenges remain in constructing high-quality domain-
specific KGs due to the complexity of unstructured texts rich in technical
terms (Liu et al., 2023). The time-intensive nature of knowledge
extraction along with the high cost of expert annotation, continues to
hinder their widespread application in maritime safety management.
2.2. Knowledge graph construction methods for the marine accident
domain
A typical KG in the marine accident domain consists of two layers: a
schema layer defining the conceptual structure and a data layer where
case-specific information is instantiated (Zhang et al., 2019). Two pri
mary ways of constructing KGs are employed: (1) top-down: an ontology
is defined as the schema first and then used to guide knowledge
extraction; (2) bottom-up: KG elements are extracted from data without
schema constraints and then followed by schema abstraction. In do
mains with well-established domain knowledge, such as maritime
safety, the top-down method enables the systematic formalization of
existing expertise into reusable ontologies, thereby facilitating struc
tured knowledge extraction and reasoning, while the bottom-up method
is widely applied in open-domain KGs (Chen, T. et al., 2022).
Schema design in the maritime context is heavily dependent on
domain expertise, requiring accurate definitions of entities, relations,
and constraints unique to shipping operations and accident causation
(Zhou et al., 2022). In contrast, the information extraction process,
typically involving entity recognition and relation extraction, follows a
more standardized pipeline. In the studies by Liu et al. (2024) and Huo
et al. (2024), domain-specific KGs were constructed for the accident
analysis in railway operations and construction sectors through a
pipeline-based extraction approach. These works laid important foun
dations for structured knowledge representation in specific domains,
although the extraction process still relied primarily on manual anno
tation and rule-based methods. With the growing volume of
multi-source marine accident reports, there is an increasing need for
automated, scalable, and robust information extraction techniques
(Zhong et al., 2023). Deep learning and statistical learning models have
exhibited satisfying performance in automated NER and relation
extraction tasks. For instance, Liu and Cheng (2024) combined Bidi
rectional Encoder Representation from Transformer (BERT), Bidirec
tional Long Short-Term Memory (Bi-LSTM), conditional random fields,
and a self-training strategy to develop a maritime-specific NER model
that achieved satisfying performance. However, these enhanced
pre-trained models often require annotated corpora and domain-specific
retraining, limiting their adaptability and scalability. To alleviate the
effort of annotation, unsupervised methods such as topic model have
been applied in extracting structured knowledge from open-ended texts
(Baburajan et al., 2022). Yet, such models may fall short in capturing
complex event structures or semantic relationships.
Recent advancements in generative LLMs provide a promising
alternative. By reframing KG construction as sequence-to-sequence
structure prediction task, LLMs can better comprehend complex task-
related knowledge with multi-head self-attention mechanisms (Ye
et al., 2022). LLMs have been successfully prompted to carry out
open-domain KG construction under Wikidata schema without anno
tated data (Feng et al., 2024; Abolhasani and Pan, 2024). Moreover,
LLM-generated KGs serve as foundational components in advanced
retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) techniques, such as GraphRAG
(Edge et al., 2024) and knowledge-augmented generation (Liang et al.,
2025). Beyond KG construction, LLMs have also demonstrated strong
capabilities in bridging semantic understanding with physical reasoning
in complex transportation systems (Liu et al., 2025). Given the
complexity and domain-specific language of marine accident data,
which includes technical terminology and regulatory references, manual
KG construction and data annotation remain costly and inefficient. Thi

2.3. Quality assessment of domain knowledge graphs
Quality assessment of the developed KG is of significant necessity for
ensuring its reliability and utility in downstream tasks. While manual
evaluation remains the most accurate approach in theory, it is resource-
intensive, non-scalable, and unsuitable for benchmarking across algo
rithms or large-scale datasets (Qi et al., 2022; Si et al., 2024).
One common strategy is the partial gold standard approach, where a
subset of data is selected as test set and manually labeled to calculate
standard metrics such as F1 score and area under curve (AUC) for
knowledge extraction quality evaluation (Paulheim, 2016). However,
this approach only assesses extraction accuracy and fails to capture
broader dimensions of KG quality. To address this, scholars have
extended general data quality measurement (i.e., intrinsic, contextual,
representation, and accessibility) to KG quality evaluation (Xue and Zou,
2022). Besides, the structure and path characteristics of KG bring
additional possibilities of developing dedicated dimensions and metrics.
Metrics regarding abundant sub-division of ontology hierarchy, the
number of attributes per class, class diversity, and overall graph
complexity have been proposed in existing studies (Seo et al., 2022).
Despite various frameworks being proposed, many are either overly
complex for practical use or lack scalability for large-scale KGs (Chen
et al., 2019). Moreover, effective evaluation should be grounded in the
domain-specific use cases. In marine accident analysis, particular
emphasis should by placed on verifying the completeness and retriev
ability of triggering factors and risk propagation paths, which are central
to safety diagnostics and causation modeling (Ma et al., 2022). Another
concern is that the LLM-based knowledge extraction may introduce
extra quality risks, such as hallucinated facts, coreference errors, and
missing context. These risks highlight the need for assessment methods
capable of detecting semantic inconsistence and verifying the fidelity of
the extracted knowledge against the original text (Zhang et al., 2024).
2.4. Research gap and workflow
Despite growing interest in developing KGs for marine accident
analysis, few automated methods have been tailored to handle the un
structured, technical, and narrative-heavy nature of accident reports.
While recent advance in generative LLMs brings potential for schema-
guided extraction, their application in the maritime safety domain re
mains underexplored. Based on the above review, three key research
gaps are identified:
(1) The development of automated pipelines specifically tailored for
structuring information from marine accident reports remains
underexplored.
(2) Establishing a comprehensive and scalable quality assessment
framework remains an important need for assessing the quality of
domain-specific KGs and advancing their applications in the
context of marine accident analysis.
(3) The impact of key configuration choices, such as decoding pa
rameters, schema, and prompt design, on the quality of LLM-
generated KGs has not been fully investigated.
To address these gaps, this study proposes an LLM-based framework
for automated KG construction and quality assessment in marine acci
dent analysis. The construction pipeline applies chain-of-thought and
few-shot prompting strategies to guide the LLM to identify the entities
and relations, and employs encoding model to generate embeddings for
the extracted knowledge. In terms of evaluation, a dual-perspective
framework is introduced. Complexity metrics assess whether the struc
tural richness of the KG contributes meaningful insights for marine ac
cident analysis. The accuracy assessment relies on LLM-aided text
reconstruction and textual similarity scoring to evaluate the faithfulness
of KG. By using these metrics, this study further explores the influencing
factors and risks of LLM-based KG construction based on comparison
analysis across various configuration settings on real-world marine ac
cident corpora.
3. Methodology
3.1. Methodological framework
The proposed framework for constructing and evaluating a KG in the
maritime safety management domain is illustrated in Fig. 1. It comprises
four core modules, which are data collection, schema construction, KG
generation, and KG quality assessment. This study primarily focuses on
the application of LLMs to the KG construction and quality assessment
processes.
First, marine accident data are sourced from official web-source
databases provided and maintained by maritime authorities. The raw
textual records are preprocessed and segmented into text chunks in a
customized corpus for safety knowledge extraction. The chunks serve as
inputs of the KG generation module.
Second, schema design is a critical prerequisite for KG development.
It defines the scope of domain knowledge by specifying marine-and
safety related concepts and identifying potential entity and relation
types. The schema provides structural guidance to the LLMs during
knowledge extraction, enabling consistent and domain-aware outputs.
Third, the process of knowledge extraction is decomposed into a
series of sub-tasks. Each sub-task is handled by a generative LLM (KG
extractor) with task-specific prompt engineering. Based on the text
chunks and schema, the model outputs subject-predicate-object (SPO)
triplets, which are stored and visualized in a graph database. Moreover,
their vector representations are generated by an embedding LLM (KG
encoder) and stored in vector database to facilitate downstream tasks.
Fourth, a dual-perspective assessment framework for maritime safety
management KG is proposed in terms of complexity and accuracy.
Complexity evaluation focuses on identifying redundancy in entities,
relations, and graph structure, ensuring the KG remains concise and free
of trivial or unnecessary components. Redundancy refers to the presence
of semantically equivalent entities, invalid or duplicated relations, and
excessive structural elements that contribute little meaningful infor
mation to the knowledge graph (Zhong et al., 2023). To assess accuracy,
a novel evaluation approach based on text reconstruction and semantic
similarity analysis is introduced. A generative LLM (text reconstructor)
is prompted to regenerate textual descriptions from sub-graphs corre
sponding to individual accident records. Semantic similarity between
the original and reconstructed text chunks serves as a proxy for the fi
delity of the KG. The assessment results guide iterative refinements to
the schema and prompt templates, facilitating continuous improvement
of KG quality in maritime safety management applications.

2.4. Research gap and workflow
Despite growing interest in developing KGs for marine accident
analysis, few automated methods have been tailored to handle the un
structured, technical, and narrative-heavy nature of accident reports.
While recent advance in generative LLMs brings potential for schema-
guided extraction, their application in the maritime safety domain re
mains underexplored. Based on the above review, three key research
gaps are identified:
(1) The development of automated pipelines specifically tailored for
structuring information from marine accident reports remains
underexplored.
(2) Establishing a comprehensive and scalable quality assessment
framework remains an important need for assessing the quality of
domain-specific KGs and advancing their applications in the
context of marine accident analysis.
(3) The impact of key configuration choices, such as decoding pa
rameters, schema, and prompt design, on the quality of LLM-
generated KGs has not been fully investigated.
To address these gaps, this study proposes an LLM-based framework
for automated KG construction and quality assessment in marine acci
dent analysis. The construction pipeline applies chain-of-thought and
few-shot prompting strategies to guide the LLM to identify the entities
and relations, and employs encoding model to generate embeddings for
the extracted knowledge. In terms of evaluation, a dual-perspective
framework is introduced. Complexity metrics assess whether the struc
tural richness of the KG contributes meaningful insights for marine ac
cident analysis. The accuracy assessment relies on LLM-aided text
reconstruction and textual similarity scoring to evaluate the faithfulness
of KG. By using these metrics, this study further explores the influencing
factors and risks of LLM-based KG construction based on comparison
analysis across various configuration settings on real-world marine ac
cident corpora.
3. Methodology
3.1. Methodological framework
The proposed framework for constructing and evaluating a KG in the
maritime safety management domain is illustrated in Fig. 1. It comprises
four core modules, which are data collection, schema construction, KG
generation, and KG quality assessment. This study primarily focuses on
the application of LLMs to the KG construction and quality assessment
processes.
First, marine accident data are sourced from official web-source
databases provided and maintained by maritime authorities. The raw
textual records are preprocessed and segmented into text chunks in a
customized corpus for safety knowledge extraction. The chunks serve as
inputs of the KG generation module.
Second, schema design is a critical prerequisite for KG development.
It defines the scope of domain knowledge by specifying marine-and
safety related concepts and identifying potential entity and relation
types. The schema provides structural guidance to the LLMs during
knowledge extraction, enabling consistent and domain-aware outputs.
Third, the process of knowledge extraction is decomposed into a
series of sub-tasks. Each sub-task is handled by a generative LLM (KG
extractor) with task-specific prompt engineering. Based on the text
chunks and schema, the model outputs subject-predicate-object (SPO)
triplets, which are stored and visualized in a graph database. Moreover,
their vector representations are generated by an embedding LLM (KG
encoder) and stored in vector database to facilitate downstream tasks.
Fourth, a dual-perspective assessment framework for maritime safety
management KG is proposed in terms of complexity and accuracy.
Complexity evaluation focuses on identifying redundancy in entities,
relations, and graph structure, ensuring the KG remains concise and free
of trivial or unnecessary components. Redundancy refers to the presence
of semantically equivalent entities, invalid or duplicated relations, and
excessive structural elements that contribute little meaningful infor
mation to the knowledge graph (Zhong et al., 2023). To assess accuracy,
a novel evaluation approach based on text reconstruction and semantic
similarity analysis is introduced. A generative LLM (text reconstructor)
is prompted to regenerate textual descriptions from sub-graphs corre
sponding to individual accident records. Semantic similarity between
the original and reconstructed text chunks serves as a proxy for the fi
delity of the KG. The assessment results guide iterative refinements to
the schema and prompt templates, facilitating continuous improvement
of KG quality in maritime safety management applications.

Marine accident investigation reports provide detailed descriptions

structured textual records often involve intricate relationships between
entities and hazardous events, making them a valuable source for safety
risk analysis. Marine authoritative bodies, such as Marine Accident
Investigation Branch (MAIB) in the U.K.,<sup>1</sup> Maritime Safety Administra-

knowledge extraction, the approach reduces the risk of cross-record
semantic interference and enhances the accuracy and traceability of
downstream KG construction and evaluation.

3.4. Knowledge graph generation
An automated pipeline for knowledge extraction and KG develop

controls. Considering the complexity of knowledge extraction, it is
decomposed into a series of sub-tasks: NER, entity standardization, and
relation extraction, with each step handled by LLMs. This design im
proves the extraction reliability by simplifying the prompt in each step
to avoid the distraction of LLM (Hwang et al., 2025). Besides, it enables
stepwise quality control and optimization, in line with the principles of
chain-of-thought.
3.4.1. Named entity recognition
NER aims to identify elements involved in each accident record. A
one-shot prompt is designed to guide the generative LLM, referred to as
the KG extractor, to extract entities and their attributes in accordance
with the schema constraints. The prompt includes role and context in
structions, the extraction schema, an annotated example, and output
formatting requirements. An example of NER prompt is provided in
Appendix B.
3.4.2. Entity standardization
Variability in the entity naming across documents may lead to
redundancy of entities, negatively impacting the scale of KG, the
calculation efficiency, and relation extraction accuracy. To address this
issue, it is necessary to transform the entity mentions into normalized
forms. The KG extractor is prompted to map overly specific terms to
standardized equivalents (e.g., timestamps, measurement units, and
common hazardous events). An example standardization prompt is
included in Appendix B.
3.4.3. Relation extraction
The final step in the extraction pipeline involves identifying the SPO
triplets among extracted entities, where the relation types are strictly in
consistent with the scheme. Emphasis is placed on producing well-
structured JSON output, with instructions to validate and, if needed,
revise the result. Appendix B includes a sample prompt for relation
extraction.

decoding parameters, which should be specified to control the
randomness and diversity of the outputs when calling LLM. Specifically,
this study tunes two parameters, temperature and top-p, to balance the
determinism and variability of LLM outputs in knowledge extraction. A
higher temperature setting promotes more diverse outputs, whereas a
lower one yields more deterministic results (Renze, 2024). The top-p
parameter constrains the token sampling to high-probability candidate
tokens, thereby enhancing output stability and stylistic consistency
(Holtzman et al., 2019). Detailed definitions of these two parameters are
provided in Appendix C.

3.5. Knowledge graph quality assessment
To ensure the reliability and utility of KG generated by LLMs, a
comprehensive quality assessment framework is proposed. The KG is
assessed in dual aspects: complexity and accuracy. Complexity evaluates
the degree of conciseness and structural efficiency of the KG, assessing
whether entities, relations, and overall graph structure are represented
in a minimal but sufficient form to enclose the underlying knowledge.
Accuracy, on the other hand, measures the fidelity of the KG to the
original text, evaluating whether the graph correctly captures the key
information expressed in the source material. These dimensions reflect a
trade-off where reduced complexity supports computational efficiency
and interpretability in downstream tasks while excessive simplification
may lead to the loss of critical information. Accordingly, quantitative
indices are developed to guide the optimization of KG construction.
3.5.1. Complexity assessment
The complexity is primarily assessed through the redundancy of
extracted entities, relations, and the graph structure.
(1) Entity Redundancy Rate
Entity redundancy is defined as the presence of multiple entities in
the KG that describe the same or highly similar instances (e.g., “strong
winds” and “high winds”) leading to unnecessary duplication in the
graph representation. Despite the implementation of entity standardi
zation, some semantically equivalent entities may still occur due to the
linguistic variability in accident reports. To assess the degree of entity
redundancy, a clustering method is employed to group potentially
equivalent entities as presented in Appendix D. The entity redundancy
rate is defined as the proportion of entities that belong to multi-member
clusters of equivalence.
(2) Relation Redundancy Rate
Two types of relation redundancy are considered, which are multiple
relations between the same entity pair and self-loops where the head and
tails of SPO triplets are identical. These relations violate the schema
constraints and reduce the graph clarity. The relation redundancy rate is
calculated as the ratio of redundant relations to the total number of
relations.
(3) Graph Structure Complexity
To assess whether the developed graph contains redundant or un
necessarily complex structures representing subordinate information in
marine accident reports, a graph-entropy measure is introduced. Graph
information entropy is a quantitative measure of the structural disorder
and information dispersion within a graph, derived from the probability
distribution of node degrees or connection strengths. A higher entropy
value indicates a more complex graph structure reflecting a greater
dispersion of information across nodes and relations. In this study, a
main causal chain is first defined, encompassing essential relations that
characterize the causation of weather-related marine accidents (e.g.,
“causes”, “exhibitedResponse”, “engagedInOperation”). Then, the graph
information entropy of the main causal chain is compared with that of
the corresponding accident-specific KG sub-graph to evaluate whether
the structural complexity required to describe the main causal chain
dominates the overall sub-graph. The mathematical definition of graph
information entropy is presented in Appendix E.

To accurately assess the semantic alignment of generated and orig
inal chunks, a sentence-level similarity assessment approach is con
ducted (Fig. 2). Both chunks are segmented into sentences. For each
sentence in the original chunk, the highest similarity score with any
sentence in the generated chunk is recorded. The average value of these
maximum scores is adopted as the ultimate similarity measure. This
approach mitigates the influence of word ordering, syntactic variation,
and structural mismatch, especially in scenarios where the recon
structed text reorganizes content without changing its core meaning.
A bi-encoder model is applied to provide more robust sentence-level
embeddings in the similarity assessment as presented in Fig. 2. In this
framework, two input sentences are encoded independently using a
shared BERT encoder. Each sentence embedding is obtained by applying
a pooling operation over the token embeddings from the final BERT
layer. The resulting fixed-size vectors can then be compared using cosine
similarity to estimate semantic closeness (Reimers and Gurevych, 2019)
Compared to cross-encoder models, bi-encoder models are less affected
by reordering or paraphrasing, making them better suited for this
evaluation setting, where semantic inclusion and coverage are the pri
mary goals (Thakur et al., 2020).

4.1. Marine accident investigation report data source
This study utilizes weather-related marine accident investigation
reports collected from two authoritative sources: the MAIB in the U.K.
and the MSA in China. The focus on weather-related cases is inten
tionally chosen to maintain the contextual consistency across samples
and to emphasize the environmental dimension of accident causation. A
detailed justification for this dataset scope has been provided in Section
(1) MAIB reports. The MAIB reports marine accidents involving UK-
registered vessels worldwide and all vessels operating in the UK
territorial waters. From a total of 1067 reports, 172 weather-
related cases from 1990 to 2023 are selected via keywords such
as “weather”, “heavy weather”, and “rough sea”. The MAIB pro
vides detailed investigation report in PDF format as well as web-
source summary of key findings and safety issues. To accommo
date the input length constraints of LLMs and minimize pre
processing complexity, the more concentrated web-source
information is extracted by web scraping techniques and used to
develop the MAIB corpus.
(2) China MSA reports. The China MSA reports marine accidents
occurring in both coastal and inland waters in China. Among the

inal chunks, a sentence-level similarity assessment approach is con

and structural mismatch, especially in scenarios where the recon
structed text reorganizes content without changing its core meaning.
A bi-encoder model is applied to provide more robust sentence-level
embeddings in the similarity assessment as presented in Fig. 2. In this
framework, two input sentences are encoded independently using a
shared BERT encoder. Each sentence embedding is obtained by applying
a pooling operation over the token embeddings from the final BERT
layer. The resulting fixed-size vectors can then be compared using cosine
similarity to estimate semantic closeness (Reimers and Gurevych, 2019)
Compared to cross-encoder models, bi-encoder models are less affected
by reordering or paraphrasing, making them better suited for this
evaluation setting, where semantic inclusion and coverage are the pri
mary goals (Thakur et al., 2020).

4.3. Comparative analysis of model performance and metric effectiveness
To validate the feasibility of the LLM-based pipeline and the effec
tiveness of the customized modeling metrics, a comparative analysis is
conducted between the LLM-based method and widely employed natu
ral language processing methods (e.g., BERT-based methods), with both
established measures and the proposed indicators.
The comparative analysis is exclusively carried out on the MAIB
corpus since the sample size of the MSA dataset is insufficient for reliable
model training and validation. Entities and relations are annotated by an
advanced LLM (ChatGPT 5) prompted via the same schema described in
Appendix A. Two BERT-based models, namely BERT-NER model and
BERT-based relation classification model, are trained on 70 % of the
dataset, with 10 % reserved for hyperparameter tuning and 20 % for
testing (Kenton and Toutanova, 2019). Table 4 summaries the evalua
tion results of BERT-based and LLM-based approaches on test set,
respectively. Both traditional metrics and the newly proposed metrics
consistently demonstrate the superior performance of applying inte
grating LLM into schema-based knowledge extraction tasks. Specifically,
the substantially higher recall can be attributed to the LLM’s stronger
contextual understanding which promotes the identification of valid
triplets. Furthermore, the enhanced performance in text reconstruction
accuracy indicates that the LLM-based method can preserve the se
mantic coherence of the original text more effectively.
This comparative evaluation also highlights the alignment and dif
ference between traditional metrics and the proposed evaluation in
dicators. While precision, recall, and F1 evaluates the fidelity of the
extracted triplets with respect to the original text, the proposed recon
struction accuracy serves a complementary role from a global semantic
perspective. The consistent performance where the LLM-based method
outperforms the BERT-based method by roughly 10 % across these two
types of metrics, i.e., macro-average F1 score and mean reconstruction
accuracy, indicates the validity of the proposed accuracy metrics as a
complementary indicator for assessing extraction quality without
relying on manually annotated data. Besides, the proposed accuracy
metrics measure the global semantic integrity of the extracted knowl
edge rather than solely on triplet-level correctness. Therefore, it is
inherently more sensitive to errors since a single incorrect or missing
triplet can disrupt the logical consistency or semantic coherence of the
whole reconstructed text. In contrast, the complexity metrics evaluate
the structural aspects of the developed KG beyond mere extraction ac
curacy. Although BERT-based approach obtains satisfactory extraction
accuracy in traditional indicators, the developed KG may still exhibit
redundant structures and limited interpretability, as reflected by the
complexity metrics. The noticeable differences in complexity metrics
between two methods highlight the necessity of incorporating structural
evaluation.

5.2. Impact of schema and prompt design on KG quality
This section discusses the impact of schema and prompt design on
the quality of generated KG for marine accident analysis. To systemat
ically assess their effects, schema and prompt revisions are implemented
in a step-wise manner, with each step introducing incremental modifi
cations. This design allows for the exploration of KG quality sensitivity
to specific configuration changes and enables the identification of key
factors that contribute to KG quality improvements.
5.2.1. KG quality assessment under incremental schema optimizations
The schema is revised by introducing more fine-grained entity and
relation types to improve extraction precision and semantic clarity. In
the first phase, broad entity categories, such as ContributingFactor, are
subdivided into specific types according to their enumerated attributes,
e.g., EquipmentFailure, HumanErrors, MaintenanceIssue. Additionally,
descriptions are incorporated to guide the KG extractor in accurately
aligning extracted entities with schema-defined concepts. In the second
phase, the generic cause relation is disaggregated into more nuanced
types, including directCauseOf, exacerbates, and resultsIn for better
distinction between primary, secondary, and compounding causal links
in accident narratives. All experiments are conducted under the default
KG extractor parameter setting (temperature is 0.1 and Top-p is 1.0).
Fig. 6 illustrates the results of accuracy and complexity evaluation
under incremental schema optimizations. Fig. 6(a) indicates that the
schema refinement improves the overall semantic fidelity of the
extracted knowledge SPO triplets. Notably, the subdivision of entity
types contributes more to similarity score improvements than modifying
relation schema. These improvements are particularly significant in
cases where semantically central information is previously missed
resulting in low similarity between original and reconstructed texts. The
gains in accuracy are attributed to the increased semantic granularity
and its constraint effect, which collectively enhance entity alignment,
reduce ambiguity, and guide the LLM to a narrower and more precise
output search space.
Fig. 6(b) shows that while overall KG accuracy gets improved, rela
tion redundancy increases and the graph becomes structurally more
complex, incorporating additional branches to represent subordinate
content. Refining the entity schema into finer-grained types improves
the accuracy of the NER sub-task by helping the model better align
mentions with their corresponding entity types, reducing errors caused
by overly broad schema. In contrast, refining relation types does not
yield the desired effect and instead introduces semantic ambiguity and
overlap between relations. For example, the relations exacerbates and
causes are both assigned between “pitching” and “container stow
collapse”. While causes typically indicates that an event leads to the
emergence of a new problem, exacerbates implies the intensification of
an already existing issue. The model, however, fails to fully distinguish
this nuance when presented with a more fine-grained relation schema,
resulting in redundant and overlapping relation assignments. Moreover,
invalid triplets, such as < crew member died, resultsIn, crew member
died>, highlight the model’s inability to detect or prevent self-loops.
These results suggest that while schema refinement enhances expres
siveness and accuracy, it may also lead to redundant or overlapping
relation assignments, especially when contextual or structural con
straints (e.g., mutual exclusivity or relation validity) are not explicitly
enforced.
